# STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS DECOLONIZATION

From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the
anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people
never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop
clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior
nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish
or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound
infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of
recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with
decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely
recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days
or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish
to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.

The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been
particularly effective over the long run.

Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

# Inpatient Decolonization Order Set:

[Mupirocin 2% ointment topically q12h M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid](orz-set-abx-chlorhexidine-mupirocin-decolonization)

topically q24h nursing text order [M] for 5 days

# Outpatient Decolonization Order Set:

Order if patient is being discharged within 5 days
[Mupirocin 2% ointment topically BID M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid](orz-set-abx-op-chlorhexidine-mupirocin-decolonization)

topically qday [M] for 5 days

# Instructions

* Patient must wear clean clothes after bathing to prevent recontamination

* Bedding and linens must be changed/cleaned daily until the end of the
decolonization protocol.
